scenario_prompt: Write the architecture section of a solution proposal, telling the migration as a narrative from the buyer's current estate to the target platform rather than as a list of components. Context: the current estate is Microsoft SQL Server (28 instances) running on Hyper-V (620 virtual machines); the target is Google Cloud, using Google Compute Engine for compute, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL for the migrated data layer, and VPC Service Controls for the new project's governance perimeter. Return only the architecture narrative text.
text:
A proposal section (architecture narrative). No customer source material was supplied for this task, so the provenance override in PF-3.3 cannot fire — every term below is judged by the deletion test alone.

## Architecture

Today, the buyer's estate runs 28 SQL Server instances across 620 virtual machines on Hyper-V — a fixed hypervisor footprint sized for peak load rather than actual demand, and a licensing and patching burden the platform team carries instance by instance [PF-2.4 GAP: quantified run-rate cost, patch/maintenance hours, or licensing spend for the current estate — not supplied]. The migration moves this estate in two coupled shifts: virtual machines to Google Compute Engine, and the SQL Server data layer to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, with the new project wrapped in a VPC Service Controls perimeter from day one rather than added afterward.

The first shift replaces the Hyper-V hosting layer with Google Compute Engine. The 620 virtual machines are re-provisioned as Compute Engine instances, sized to the workload rather than to a static hypervisor cluster, so the buyer moves from provisioning for peak to provisioning for measured demand [PF-2.4 GAP: target instance count or right-sizing ratio after migration — not supplied]. This is the before/after this section anchors on: before, capacity is fixed by the Hyper-V cluster's physical limits; after, capacity is Compute Engine capacity, adjusted per workload.

The second shift is the harder one: the 28 SQL Server instances move to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, which means both a platform change and an engine change. This is not a lift-and-shift of the database layer — schema, stored procedures, and application connection logic must be assessed for SQL Server-to-PostgreSQL compatibility before any instance is cut over [PF-2.4 GAP: which of the 28 instances have already been assessed for T-SQL-to-PostgreSQL compatibility, and the resulting migration complexity tiering — not supplied]. The buyer needs a managed, patched, backed-up PostgreSQL service without operating the underlying database servers; Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL delivers that as the means, taking over the operational work the current 28-instance estate requires today.

Once compute and data sit in Google Cloud, the project boundary becomes the governance boundary. The buyer needs a way to keep data inside the new environment from leaving through misconfigured IAM grants or exfiltration paths, even as more services are added; VPC Service Controls establishes that perimeter around the new project from the outset, rather than as a control retrofitted once the migration is complete.

Read end to end: the buyer moves from a hypervisor-bound estate of 28 SQL Server instances and 620 VMs, sized and secured instance by instance, to a Google Cloud project where compute scales on Compute Engine, the data layer runs as managed PostgreSQL on Cloud SQL, and VPC Service Controls enforces the perimeter around all of it from the first day the project exists.
